sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Contingency analysis entails the examination of the
implementation of outages for transmission lines and gen-
erators, whether individually or simultaneously. An outage
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Vitor Monteiro
.
experienced by a single entity at one time is known as
an n-1 contingency. When two entities experience outages
concurrently, it is called an n-2 contingency, also known as
a simultaneous outage. Likewise, the contingency is iden-
tified as an n-k contingency for ‘k’ outages. Conducting
n-1 contingency analysis is more feasible in power systems
compared to n-k contingency analysis, as n-1 failures are

considerably more probable in real-world scenarios, while
n-k events denote rare, simultaneous outages that are sta-
tistically less likely. Furthermore, industry standards, such
as those established by the North American Electric Reli-
ability Corporation (NERC), require compliance with n-1
contingency protocols as a foundational criterion for ensur-
ing system reliability, whereas n-k analysis is not typically
mandated for routine operations. Additionally, designing sys-
tems to accommodate all potential n-k contingencies would
necessitate excessive redundancy and substantial infrastruc-
ture investments, rendering such approaches economically
impractical. In instances where n-k analysis is warranted,
such as in resilience assessments, it is generally confined to
selected credible combinations through heuristic or proba-
bilistic screening methodologies. Consequently, n-1 analysis
remains the predominant and standard approach for power
system planning and operation. The focus of this paper is
on the evaluation of system performance parameters by the
proposed methodology in estimating DA UC in the presence
of n-1 thermal generator contingencies.
The dependable operation of power systems is of utmost
importance to ensure an uninterrupted electricity supply, par-
ticularly as modern grids increasingly integrate renewable
energy sources and face escalating demands. A significant
challenge in maintaining grid stability involves addressing
potential contingencies that may disrupt power generation.
The N-1 contingency criteria, assuming the failure of a single
generator or transmission line, are a widely adopted stan-
dard in power system planning and operation. It guarantees
the system’s functionality even when a critical component
fails. Understanding the impact of these contingencies on the
system’s operational decisions is crucial for thermal power
generators, which will continue to hold a substantial role in
global power generation for some years till they are replaced
by green energy [1].
UC, which determines the optimal scheduling of genera-
tion units to meet the forecasted demand at the lowest cost,
is one of the primary decisions affected by N-1 contingen-
cies. A robust UC schedule must account for the possibility
of unforeseen outages in thermal generators while ensuring
the availability of sufficient reserve capacity to uphold sys-
tem reliability. However, thermal generator outages can give
rise to significant operational challenges, including increased
generation costs, grid instability, and the need for rapid
adjustments in generation from alternative sources. V arious
studies on this topic propose different approaches to effec-
tively carry out UC in the presence of n-1 contingencies.
Numerous solutions have been proposed in previous research
to address the issue of n-1 contingencies. One approach
involves activating additional power plants to compensate for
the outage of conventional generators. Specifically, gas power
plants are employed in UC to ensure an uninterrupted power
supply in the presence of n-1 generator contingencies [2].
Another option is to utilize the individual contributions or
coordinated operation of interconnected or integrated system
components. For instance, a study investigates the coordi-
nated operation of a combined heat & electricity system with
renewable energy sources to enhance the flexibility of the
power system in conducting energy dispatch under uncertain
component states [3]. The modelling of uncertain outages
of individual generators becomes necessary for developing
a comprehensive probability distribution that proportionately
affects UC scheduling and costs [4]. Thus, it holds signifi-
cant importance in estimating DA UC costs in the event of
generator contingencies.
Additionally, transmission line switching has been
explored as a means to enhance system performance in
optimal power flow problems when faced with n-1 contin-
gencies [5]. Moreover, integrated renewable energy sources
serve as alternative power sources to maintain system reli-
ability and flexibility when determining optimal UC under
n-1 contingencies [6]. While there has been research on n-1
generator contingencies, studies have also been conducted to
investigate the impacts of n-1 transmission line contingencies
on UC [7]. Power system security assessment for multiple
contingencies has been empirically demonstrated in prior
research [8]. However, most of these works focus on specific
contingency management strategies or integrated systems,
lacking a unified methodology to assess system-wide per-
formance metrics—such as criticality, robustness, reliability,
and operating margin—in the context of DA UC under N-1
generator outages.
The occurrence of n-1 generator contingencies has the
potential to disrupt the supply-demand equilibrium, poten-
tially leading to an inability to meet load demands. This
situation necessitates a comprehensive analysis of system
reliability, criticality, and the available operating margin to
facilitate appropriate preparations for dispatch based on the
DA UC results. This paper conducts an impact analysis on
the reliability and robustness of DA UC decisions under n-
1 thermal generator contingencies. By examining how the
failure of individual thermal generators affects the optimal
scheduling of generation units, our objective is to evaluate the
grid’s capacity to maintain supply-demand balance and meet
load requirements during such challenging conditions.
The reliability of the system under these circumstances
is assessed using metrics such as LOLP , Loss of Load
Expectation (LOLE), etc. as established in previous stud-
ies [9]. Before estimating LOLP , probabilistic analyses are
performed to evaluate the probabilities of generation unavail-
ability under various n-1 generator contingencies [10], [11].
In this paper, we estimate the reliability of the n-1 generator
contingency-based DA UC results using LOLP through the
proposed methodology. Existing works that estimate LOLP
generally do so for planning or risk analysis. However, very
few integrate such probabilistic reliability indices within the
context of DA UC execution under generator contingencies,
which is necessary for system preparedness.
For the estimation of DA UC scheduling and associated
costs, we employ Dynamic Programming (DP) optimization

in this study. In comparison to novel heuristic and metaheuris-
tic approaches, DP optimization yields the most optimal
solution [12]. Given the critical role of thermal generators
in supplying base load and balancing intermittent renewable
energy sources, this research provides valuable insights into
how power system operators can formulate more resilient
scheduling strategies for the following day in response to
contingencies. By incorporating n-1 generator contingencies
into the unit commitment planning process, power systems

quantification of DA UC plans under N-1 generator outages
is yet to be formalized.
A. RESEARCH GAPS
Despite several advancements in UC and contingency analy-
sis, the following significant research gaps persist:
i) Absence of an Integrated System Performance Frame-
work: Current research predominantly concentrates on
discrete elements such as cost optimization, reserve
scheduling, or generator coordination during contin-
gencies. However, there is a conspicuous lack of a
comprehensive methodology that simultaneously eval-
uates system criticality, robustness, reliability, and
operating margin in the context of N-1 generator con-
tingencies impacting DA UC.
ii) Lack of Established Metrics for Generator-Level Criti-
cality in DA UC: Criticality indices have been proposed
for system components utilizing methodologies such as
FMEA, SOC, or topological analysis. However, these
frameworks are not specifically designed to assess
the criticality of individual thermal generators in DA
UC under N-1 contingency scenarios. A formalized
mechanism to rank and quantify generator criticality
is necessary to facilitate contingency-aware scheduling
decisions.
iii) Inadequate Evaluation of Robustness for
Contingency-Based DA UC Schedules: Robustness
metrics are typically applied to cascading failures,
control systems, or network topologies. Nevertheless,
the resilience of DA UC schedules in the context of
generator outage scenarios has not been subjected to
comprehensive analysis within the existing literature.
This gap restricts the capacity to assess the effective-
ness of these schedules in mitigating disturbances or
sustaining operational feasibility during contingencies.
iv) Limited Incorporation of Probabilistic Reliability Met-
rics into DA UC Performance Evaluation: Although
probabilistic indices such as Loss of Load Probability
(LOLP) and Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) are
well-established in power system reliability analyses,
there is a scarcity of studies that directly integrate these
measures into the evaluation of DA UC schedules.
This integration is crucial for assessing the real-world
viability of commitments exposed to contingencies.
v) Absence of a Quantified Operating Margin Metric
for Dispatch Feasibility: Most existing research on
DA UC emphasizes the attainment of cost-minimizing
schedules under predicted conditions, without provid-
ing a clear quantitative assessment of how closely the
resultant schedule aligns with the system’s operational
limits. This limitation hampers operators’ capacity to
determine whether the schedule will remain feasible in
the face of unforeseen contingencies.
In light of the aforementioned considerations, this study
delineates several significant research gaps in the extant
literature that impede the reliability and preparedness of DA
UC plans in the event of generator outages. These gaps
encompass the absence of integrated system performance
evaluations, generator-level criticality metrics, robustness
analyses of UC schedules, probabilistic reliability assess-
ments, and explicit operating margin estimations. Collec-
tively, these deficiencies constitute the basis for the proposed
methodology. Addressing these issues is crucial for improv-
ing real-time dispatch feasibility and enhancing long-term
system resilience in the context of N-1 thermal generator
contingencies.
B. CONTRIBUTIONS
This study presents a structured framework for evaluating
system performance and preparedness for real-time dispatch
in the presence of N-1 thermal generator contingencies.
The proposed methodology introduces both quantitative
and qualitative tools for assessing key system performance
indicators—criticality,robustness,reliability,and operating
margin—within a contingency-aware DA UC framework.
The main contributions are as follows:
i) A novel methodology for generator-level criticality
assessment is developed to identify and quantify the oper-
ational impact of individual N-1 generator outages on DA
UC schedules. This enables the classification and ranking
of contingencies based on their severity, directly addressing
the lack of generator-specific criticality metrics in existing
literature.
ii) A CM-based robustness evaluation is proposed to quan-
tify the system’s ability to sustain outages without violating
operational limits. The CM metric supports the identifica-
tion of weak and robust buses, addressing the current gap
in robustness analysis of DA UC schedules under generator
contingencies.
iii) Integration of probabilistic reliability analysis using the
LOLP index provides a quantitative assessment of system
reliability across varying levels of Spinning Reserve (SR).
This contributes to bridging the gap between reliability esti-
mation and DA UC performance evaluation.
iv) A new operating margin metric is formulated to
determine the residual capacity available beyond commit-
ted reserves, reflecting the system’s real-time feasibility and
resilience. This explicitly addresses the need for quantifying
dispatch margin under stress conditions, which is currently
absent in conventional DA UC approaches.
In summary, this work addresses multiple gaps in existing
literature by developing a comprehensive framework for eval-
uating system performance in contingency-aware DA UC.
It introduces new metrics for assessing generator critical-
ity, system robustness, reliability via LOLP , and operating
margin—each of which is essential for reliable and eco-
nomically feasible real-time dispatch planning under N-1
generator contingencies.
The structure of this paper is as follows: The pro-
posed methodology for assessing the performance of n-1
contingency-based DA UC is discussed in Section II. The
mathematical formulation of DA UC with the constraints,

Section IV provides an outline of the Case Studies employed
to simulate the proposed n-1 contingency-based DA UC. The
optimization technique employed for DA UC is mentioned
in Section V. The following section presents the data for the
IEEE RTS and the underlying assumptions for performing the
proposed analysis. The results, along with their analysis, are
presented in Section VII. Lastly, Section VIII offers conclu-
sions.

sections.title: PROPOSED METHODOLOGY
sections.text:
The proposed approach addresses key gaps in current lit-
erature by incorporating generator-level contingency impact
assessment, robustness quantification, probabilistic reliabil-
ity estimation, and operational margin evaluation into the DA
UC framework. The methodology comprises the following
steps.
Step1: Identification of Critical n-1 Generator Contingen-
cies
In the first step, N-1 contingency simulations are con-
ducted for each thermal generator to identify outages that
significantly impact DA UC feasibility or economic perfor-
mance.
(i) Contingency Impact Assessment: Generator outages
are classified as critical if they cause operational infea-
sibility or substantial cost increases in the DA UC
solution.
(ii) DA UC Modeling: The DA UC problem is for-
mulated and solved using DP for all contingency
scenarios. The severity of each contingency is assessed
based on the incurred operational cost or failure to
meet the load. This directly addresses the lack of
generator-specific criticality assessment methods in
existing contingency-aware UC studies.
Step 2: Identification of Weak Buses Associated with Crit-
ical Contingencies
Upon identifying critical generator outages, the next step
involves determining the weak buses, those most sensitive to
associated failures. Weak buses are identified based on their
susceptibility to overloads or operational stress during DA
UC under critical contingencies. These buses are generally
connected to or impacted by the failed generator units.
This step extends contingency analysis to the spatial
dimension of the network, addressing the research gap in
linking contingency severity to localized grid vulnerability.
Step 3: Estimation of System Robustness and Identification
of Robust Buses
To quantify system robustness, this step identifies stable
N-1 contingencies and the corresponding robust buses.
i) Stable Contingency Classification: Generator outages
that do not disrupt UC feasibility and/or do not increase
cost significantly are deemed stable.
ii) Robust Bus Identification: Buses connected to genera-
tors under stable contingencies are classified as robust.
These nodes demonstrate the system’s inherent ability
to absorb disturbances without compromising opera-
tional integrity.
This addresses the research gap regarding the absence of
system-wide and bus-level robustness metrics for DA UC
schedules.
Step 4: Reliability Estimation Using LOLP
This step integrates LOLP as a probabilistic metric to
evaluate the reliability of DA UC outcomes under generator
outages.
Based on probabilistic modeling of generator unavailabil-
ity, the LOLP index is computed for each scenario. This
reflects the likelihood that the system fails to meet demand
under given contingencies and reserve conditions.
This contributes to the limited body of research that con-
nects probabilistic reliability metrics with UC outcomes in a
contingency-aware context.
Step 5: Evaluation of the Operating Margin
The final step involves the evaluation of the Operating
Margin, a newly proposed metric that measures the system’s
additional capacity beyond committed reserves, capable of
absorbing future contingencies.
The Operating Margin is calculated as the difference
between the maximum allowable LOLP and the estimated
LOLP value. A positive margin indicates headroom for addi-
tional load or contingencies; a negative margin implies risk
of dispatch failure.
This metric directly supports system operators in assessing
real-time dispatch feasibility, bridging the gap in quantifying
flexibility and resilience of DA UC schedules under stress.
The proposed methodology is illustrated in Fig. 1.

D. RELIABILITY ASSESSMENT via LOLP
The reliability of a system can be evaluated through the use
of reliability indices. V arious electricity regulatory authorities
across different countries establish the maximum allowable
limits for generator contingency reliability indices, such as
LOLP and LOLE. A high probability of load loss indicates
that generation is insufficient to meet demand, thereby sug-
gesting a lower reliability of DA UC in the presence of the
considered generator contingencies. Conversely, reliability is
deemed higher when the probability of load loss remains
below the established maximum allowable limit.

F. ESTIMATING THE CRITICALITY AND ROBUSTNESS OF
THE SYSTEM FOR n-1 GENERATOR CONTINGENCY BASED
DA UC
The process of identifying system criticality points and sys-
tem robustness is illustrated in Fig. 1. Throughout the paper,
this process is employed to identify the weak and robust buses
of the system in response to n-1 generator contingencies.
If the DA UC is feasible based on the fulfillment of the
supply-demand metric, the outcome may be either an eco-
nomical or uneconomical DA UC. The stable contingencies,
which result in an economical DA UC, can help identify the
robust buses of the network. Conversely, if the DA UC is
uneconomical, critical contingencies are identified to deter-
mine the weak buses.

sections.title: TECHNIQUE FOR DETERMINING N-1 GENERATOR
sections.text:
CONTINGENCY BASED DA UC WITH VARYING
CONTINGENCY MARGINS
This paper utilizes DP [28], [29] to determine the optimal
solution for DA UC, specifically focusing on analyzing the
costs associated with n-1 generator contingencies, referred to
as n-1 generator contingency-based DA UC. Additionally, the
effects of decreasing CM from ten percent to zero percent on
the costs of n-1 generator contingency-based DA UC are ana-
lyzed to identify the optimal CM in the event of n-1 generator
outages. The reliability of n-1 generator contingency-based
DA UC results is estimated as per the formulation mentioned
in the previous section. The economic performance of n-1
generator contingency-based DA UC is evaluated by compar-
ing these results with those obtained without any contingency.
Fig. 1 illustrates the process flow of the applied technique.
A. BASE CASE OR PRE-CONTINGENCY DA UC COST
ANAL YSIS WITHOUT n-1 GENERATOR CONTINGENCIES
To assess the economic performance of n-1 generator
contingency-based DA UC, it is necessary to evaluate the
UC costs for the system in the absence of any contingencies,
referred to as the ‘‘Base Case’’ in this paper. The costs of
the pre-contingency DA UC are then determined, forming the
basis for the Base Case.

B. DA UC COSTS FOR n-1 GENERATOR CONTINGENCIES
WITH CM OPTIMIZATION-CASE 1 AND CASE 2
The n-1 generator contingency-based DA UC analysis
involves the following steps, as explained below:
Case 1: Perform DA UC analysis for the various n-1 gen-
erator contingencies in the system
i) Simulate the outage of 1 generator, one by one. For
each generator contingency, run the DA UC with the
mentioned constraints and CM corresponding to a ten
percent SR. Compile the DA UC costs.
ii) Identify the stable and critical contingencies as per the
proposed methodology (Fig. 2).
iii) Identify the corresponding robust and weak generator
buses as per the proposed methodology (Fig. 2). Rank
the weak buses in increasing order with the increasing
value of percentage rise in UC costs. Rank the robust
buses in the opposite sequence.
Case 2: Decrease the CM in steps from ten percent to zero
percent and perform n-1 generator contingency-based DA UC
analysis again to find out the optimal CM.
i) Simulate the outage of 1 generator, one by one. For
each generator contingency, run the DA UC with the
mentioned constraints, decreasing values of SR from
ten percent to zero percent. Compile the DA UC costs
for the CM variation of 10%, 8%, 5%, and 0% with
respect to the various n-1 generator contingencies.
ii) Perform steps (ii) and (iii) of Case 1.
iii) Identify which value of CM gives most economical DA
UC when n-1 generator contingencies are simulated.

sections.title: METHODOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR
sections.text:
IMPLEMENTING THREE CASE STUDIES TO EVALUATE
SYSTEM PERFORMANCE UNDER N-1 GENERATOR
CONTINGENCY IN DA UC ANALYSIS
The framework for the implementation of the three case
studies, as delineated in Table 1, seeks to evaluate system
performance under simulated n-1 generator contingencies,
as depicted in Figure 3. The analysis is conducted in two
distinct stages. The first stage comprises the assessment of n-

sections.title: 1 generator contingency-based DA UC, with its performance
sections.text:
compared to the Base Case to enhance the understanding
of the impacts of contingencies. The second stage entails a
validation process wherein the results obtained from the gen-
erator contingency-based DA UC are corroborated through a
load loss probability analysis, focusing exclusively on single
generator contingencies. This is accomplished via the Loss of
Load Probability evaluation for individual generator outages.
Subsequently, the results of the LOLP analysis are utilized
to estimate system reliability and the operating margin. The
outcomes of the DA UC, in conjunction with the LOLP
estimation and the evaluation of operating margins, serve
as critical metrics for assessing system performance. This
comprehensive evaluation aids in determining the feasibility
of load dispatch for the forthcoming day, ensuring that the
system remains within established operational limits while
upholding the requisite level of reliability.

sections.title: SYSTEM DESCRIPTION
sections.text:
This work examines the use of the 24-bus, 26-generator
IEEE Reliability Test System (RTS) [30], [31], [32], [33] for

S. Jain, N. Kanwar: Evaluation of System Performance for Load Dispatch Feasibility
performing n-1 generator contingency-based UC with opti-
mal CM allocation. The single line diagram of IEEE RTS is
shown in Fig. 4.
A. ASSUMPTIONS FOR CARRYING OUT THE PROPOSED
ANAL YSIS
The n-1 generator contingency is performed with the follow-
ing assumptions:
i) For n-1 contingency, failure of one unit is considered
in the system with no simultaneous outages of single
units of other rating generators. This is done since the
simultaneous outage of two or more different rating
generators is practically not possible to avoid shutdown
& startup costs as well as maintenance. Moreover, the
periodical maintenance of all generators in a running
condition is ensured to avoid such forced outages.
ii) The conditional probability of ‘one’ generator outage
with other generators is not considered.
The evaluation of LOLP is based on the following
assumptions:
i) LOLP is assessed by considering the forced outage of
only one generating unit at a time.
ii) The paper does not take into account simultaneous
outages of single units with different ratings connected
to different bus numbers.
iii) Outages of more than one unit are not considered for
LOLP calculation.
iv) Additionally, the conditional probabilities between
various generators are not modeled to simplify the
analysis. Furthermore, their impact on the results is
considered negligible, and therefore, they are disre-
garded in the analysis.
v) LOLPmax, as specified by the Central Electricity
Authority (CEA) of India, is 0.05 [34]. This value can
be verified from the official website data repository
of the CEA. Similarly, the US Department of Energy
specifies a LOLPmax of 0.002 (equivalent to 0.1/year)
[35], while the European Union Standards specify a
LOLPmax of 0.008 [36]. These values can be verified
from the respective official website data repositories.
For this study, assuming the system is operating under
strict limits, a LOLPmax of 0.05 is considered
B. SYSTEM DATA
The system comprises 26 thermal generators, which are
assigned indexes ranging from 1 to 26, connected to a 24-bus
system. The data from the IEEE RTS is cited in references[1],
[2], [14], and [15]. The data utilized in this study are presented
in Table 2. The bus numbers (‘b’) to which generators of spe-
cific capacity are connected are listed in column 1 of Table 2.
The number of generating units connected to each bus num-
ber, their respective indexes, and the maximum capacity of a
single unit are indicated in columns 2, 3, and 4, respectively.
The final column provides the maximum generation capacity
available at each bus ‘b’.
TABLE 1. Cases for the performed analysis.
The total available capacity of the system is 3105 MW.
However, the capacity available for UC or load dispatch will
be determined using Equations (1) to (9) with other constraint
formulations referred from [27]. Therefore, considering the
default 10% SR corresponding to CM of 310.5 MW (approx-
imately 310 MW), the capacity available for estimating DA
UC is 2795 MW. This value will be used as a reference for
the Base Case and Case 1.
In Case 2, the capacity available for dispatch can be sum-
marized as follows:
Case 2(a): The 8% SR of each generator corresponds to

available for DA UC will be increased to 2857 MW.
Case 2(b): The 5% SR of each generator renders CM
of 155 MW unavailable to the operator for dispatch. As a
result, the capacity available for DA UC becomes 2950 MW.
Case 2(c): An SR of 0% i.e. zero CM indicates that all
generators in the system are loaded to their full capacity.
In this scenario, the capacity available for DA UC is 3105
MW.
The generator data, including the fuel cost coefficients a i,
bi, c i, active power limits, ramp up rate, ramp down rate,

sections.title: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
This section presents the DA UC cost results for the Base
Case, Case 1, and Case 2, followed by an evaluation of
the system performance parameters as previously formulated
and discussed. Subsequently, a feasibility assessment is con-
ducted regarding the load dispatch for the following day,
informed by the system performance observed during the
DA UC simulation under executed n-1 generator contin-
gencies. The findings of the implemented methodology are
detailed in Section VII-A. An analysis of these results is
provided in Section VII-B, focusing on the practical appli-
cation of DA UC for economically dispatching the loads
for the following day and preparing the necessary measures
in advance to ensure reliable system operation within safe
limits.
A. COMPILATION OF DA UC RESUL TS
After compiling the severe n-1 generator contingencies, the
DA UC program is simulated with the outage of the one
generator corresponding to each severe contingency. To esti-
mate the increase in costs (if any) for each n-1 generator
contingency, the pre-contingency or ‘Base Case’ UC costs are
compared with these costs. The DA UC costs are estimated
for the following cases:
i) Base Case
ii) Case 1
iii) Case 2
This is followed by reliability analysis of the n-1
contingency-based DA UC results via LOLP .
1) BASE CASE
In the ‘Base Case’, the optimization of DA UC is performed
via the DP technique with the mentioned constraints, when
n-1 generator contingencies are not considered in the system,
with a CM of 10%. Since the analysis is performed before
simulating contingencies, it is termed as ‘pre-contingency’
analysis which forms the basis of comparison for the other
2 cases. The original system of IEEE RTS is utilized for
conducting the analysis. The cumulative DA UC costs for
each hour ‘t’ of the next day are estimated for the system via
DP . DP is executed in MA TLAB via coding, including all the
mentioned constraints, and compiled in Table 4.

B. RELIABILITY ESTIMATION OF n-1 GENERATOR
CONTINGENCY BASED DA UC
The reliability of the Case 1 and Case 2 results is estimated
via the reliability index LOLP . For estimating the reliability of
the obtained DA UC results under n-1 generator contingency,
LOLP is calculated. To calculate the LOLP index, the genera-
tion unavailability needs to be evaluated from the perspective

referred to in [10] and [11].

D. ANAL YSIS OF RESUL TS
The results obtained are judged and analyzed utilizing the
aforementioned data. The analyses derived from the simu-
lated cases are derived and summarized in this section.
1) COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF D.A. U.C. COSTS FOR THE
N-1 GENERATOR CONTINGENCIES WITH CRITICALITY AND
ROBUSTNESS ANALYSIS OF SYSTEM
a: BASE CASE
The DA UC cost for the considered IEEE RTS system when
optimized via DP is found to be $ 774100. This cost forms
the basis of comparison for the n-1 contingency-based DA
UC with varying SR, which are analyzed in Cases 1 and 2.

The Base Case cost of DA UC is quite low, i.e., without any
generator outage, the system runs smoothly.
b: CASE 1
Even with a 10% SR, it is still possible to perform DA UC
based on n-1 generator outages. These contingencies do not
pose a significant threat to the supply-demand balance, and
real-time load dispatch can still be effectively carried out
despite the large increase in DA UC costs in the case of
one generator outage on buses 18, 21, and 23. N-1 generator
contingency on bus numbers 2 and 7 results in a negligible
increase in UC costs. The remaining buses don’t experience
any increase in costs despite the generator outage.
The percentage variation of DA UC costs obtained in
Case 1 with respect to Base Case results is represented in
Table 5. The percentage variation in DA UC costs for Cases
2(a) and 2(b) is also the same. A graphical representation of
the percentage variation of these costs with respect to the nine
simulated contingencies is shown in Fig. 7.
After determining the percentage variation in UC costs
for contingencies indexed from 1 to 9, they are subsequently
ranked from 1 to 4 based on the descending order of their DA
UC costs. These rankings are graphically presented in Fig. 8.
Fig. 8 illustrates the ranking of nine simulated n-1 gen-
erator contingencies, specifically for Case 1 and the two
conditions of Case 2- (a) and (b), when CM is 248 MW
and 155 MW, respectively, as illustrated in Section VI-B.
Case 1 and Case 2(a), 2(b) are analyzed together due to
the identical DA UC costs observed between Case 1 and the
aforementioned conditions of Case 2, as confirmed by the
data presented in Table6. It is evident that the highest capacity
generator outage, specifically 400 MW at buses 18 and 21,
poses the greatest risk to the system. Thus, buses 18 and
21 are the weakestin the network. Consequently,contingen-
cies (Cy)6 and 7 are ranked as the most critical, occupying
the top position. Contingency 1, on the other hand, does not
exhibit any increase in DA UC costs, thereby posing no threat
to the system. Contingencies 4 and 5 demonstrate a decrease
in costs below the Base Case UC cost, making them the
most stable contingencies. Thus, bus 13 and 15 serve as the
robust buses in the network.
Thus, the n-1 generator contingency, even with 10% SR,
doesn’t have any significant impact on DA UC implemen-
tation since the supply-demand balance is maintained. The
only change observed is the increase in DA UC costs for
a few contingencies. The above analysis is done for 10%
SR with a CM of 310.5 MW. However, to utilize CM in
a better manner for further reducing DA UC costs in the
presence of n-1 generator contingencies, CM is reduced in
steps from 248 MW to 0 MW in Case 2.
c: CASE 2
The post-contingency costs are quite high for the
high-capacity generators of 350 MW and 400 MW. For the
generators of 300 MW and 450 MW, their outage leads
to high UC costs, since the other higher cost generators
need to be committed in their place to deliver power to
the required load demand. However, with the full operating
reserve consumption during the n-1 contingency, i.e., when
CM is 0 MW, the UC costs drop significantly compared to
those of Case 1.

to be analyzed for the following three conditions, as specified
in Section VI-B:
